A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlashBlock and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Trado accuracy and throughput experiments, sparse-attention comparisons, ablations, and LongLive video evaluations, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds LongBench evaluations, overhead measurements, and comparisons with Pyramid Attention Broadcast.

M1.justification: The attention decomposition, selective reuse rules, log-space composition, sparse-attention integration, and distillation objectives remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves from Appendix C to Section 4.3 without procedural changes; the optional LoRA adaptation was already present.

E1.justification: v3 adds LongBench evaluation to the retained reasoning, coding, and VBench2 coverage (Appendix A, Tables 7–8). This is a limited documented extension: only aggregate LongBench scores are provided. The five VBench dimensions used for the new PAB comparison already appear in v1.

E2.justification: v3 adds Pyramid Attention Broadcast (PAB), evaluated with three broadcast schedules against dense attention and FlashBlock on five VBench dimensions (Table 9). The existing Trado, SparseD, LongLive, and SpargeAttention comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The reported video reuse threshold changes from gamma = 0.9 to 0.85, and FlashBlock's reported attention density changes from 55% to 45%. Added experiments introduce training-free LLaDA-2.0 evaluation using SGLang, PAB schedule comparisons, and overhead measurements across specified batch sizes and context lengths. The original Trado protocols remain; the PDFs do not establish whether the revised video settings reflect reruns or corrections.

E4.justification: New Table 5 measures aggregation time and additional memory across context lengths and batch sizes, empirically examining overhead previously discussed through complexity arguments. It reports approximately 0.07 ms aggregation cost and memory overhead below 0.11%. The threshold/distillation ablation, attention-similarity analyses, and qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a defined uncertainty-estimation procedure. The new tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantive numerical evidence on overhead, LongBench, and PAB. Tables 7–8 report dense versus FlashBlock LongBench averages of 48.98 versus 47.96 for LLaDA-2.0, with 1.33x decoding speedup, and 34.54 versus 34.20 for Trado. Video timings also change throughout v1 Table 5/v3 Table 4: dense attention time changes from 23.02 to 19.89 seconds and FlashBlock from 14.43 to 12.46 seconds, while quality scores remain identical. These revisions do not establish same-setting gains because reported video settings also change.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(12), the attention decomposition and composition derivation, and the computational and memory complexity arguments are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same core claims about attention stability, block-external caching, sparse-attention compatibility, and quality preservation. The headline 1.44x throughput and approximately 1.6x attention-speedup claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix A interprets the LLaDA-2.0 results as evidence that training-free reuse transfers beyond Trado. It explains the PAB comparison through FlashBlock's avoidance of reusing unstable block-internal attention and explicitly limits that comparison to five VBench subsets because of time constraints. Existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses approximately three days on two NVIDIA A100 GPUs for distillation and explicitly states that the base weights remain frozen. It also identifies SGLang for the added LLaDA-2.0 experiment. The existing rank-32 LoRA configuration, 5,000 iterations, and training dataset are unchanged; these disclosures do not establish a changed training procedure.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to LLaDA-2.0 and Pyramid Attention Broadcast and distinguishes FlashBlock's component-specific reuse from PAB's attention-output broadcasting in Appendix A. The main related-work section and broader positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v3 moves the inference algorithm into the methodology, reorders the latency discussion, adds an appendix section, removes a duplicated SparseD sentence, and corrects the running header and publication information. These are localized structural and editorial changes.

P2.justification: v3 adds four tables for overhead, two LongBench evaluations, and PAB comparisons. It enlarges the main video-results table from one column to full width and relocates the algorithm and several existing displays. The ten figures retain their content, including the same qualitative video frames.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v3 better supports practical efficiency and applicability through measured overhead, LongBench evaluation on another diffusion model, and a direct attention-caching comparator. Disclosure of distillation cost also improves transparency. These gains are bounded by sparse documentation of the new LongBench experiments and unexplained video-timing revisions accompanying changed settings, so the overall improvement is useful but limited.
